title: Where the line came from
hookLine: a line that isn't in Valmiki is now an everyday word, and Hindus are at home with that
tomorrow: A holy man at the door
last: PRANAM: BOW TO THE GOD IN THEM.

lines: A LIMIT YOU MUST NOT CROSS.
SO WHERE DID IT COME FROM?
cards: Open an Indian newspaper and you may find it in a headline. A court warns the government not to cross the Lakshman rekha. A columnist says a joke crossed the Lakshman rekha.
A parent tells a teenager: curfew is eleven, that's the Lakshman rekha. Lakshmana's line, a limit you must not cross, has become everyday speech. Yet in Valmiki's Ramayana, the line doesn't exist.
So where did it come from?

teach.b: The Ramayana was never only one book. It was retold in Tamil, Bengali, Telugu, Hindi and other languages, in songs, plays, temple carvings and village performances. The line belongs to that later life.
One well-known witness is Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the retelling in Awadhi, an older form of Hindi. Even there, the line isn't drawn in the forest scene.
It's mentioned later, by Ravana's wife, Mandodari, pleading with him before the war: you couldn't even cross the little line Rama's younger brother drew. How will you face Rama?
From hints like that, storytellers grew the scene. Ramlila performers acted it out, painters painted it, television put it before huge audiences. So which is the real Ramayana?
Here's the teaching, and it's deeply Hindu: there's no single official version.
Valmiki's Sanskrit, Kamban's Tamil, Tulsidas's Awadhi, a Ramlila in a temple hall: Hindus have long kept many tellings side by side and loved each one.
Tulsidas says it himself: Hari ananta, Hari katha ananta.
God is endless, and endless are God's stories, told by the saints in many ways.
Retelling isn't getting it wrong. It's how devotion keeps the story breathing. Valmiki's forest spirits and the later line in the dust carry the same brother's care.

how: The Lakshman rekha is a common phrase in Hindi and Indian English for a limit not to be crossed, and the drawn line is a familiar scene in Ramlila. Hindus keep many Ramayanas, in Sanskrit, Tamil, Awadhi and other languages, and read and stage them side by side.

games.q: where the line came from — tap the pairs.
p: no line: the forest spirits as witness

s: in Tulsidas, the line is mentioned by Ravana's wife
Mandodari reminds Ravana he couldn't cross the little line.
the line is a modern invention of television
it's older than television: Tulsidas already mentions it, and Ramlila stages it too.
the 'real' Ramayana is Valmiki's, and the rest are mistakes
Hindus keep many tellings side by side; Tulsidas says God's stories are endless.

games.q: at the temple Ramlila, a visiting uncle says the Lakshman rekha scene should be cut because Valmiki doesn't have it. what fits today's teaching?
o: keep it: Hindus have long held many tellings, and this is one way Rama's story is loved.
cut it: only the oldest version counts.
keep it, but tell everyone Valmiki has it too.
games.why: many Ramayanas, one Rama. the line isn't in Valmiki, and it still belongs to how Hindus tell the story. just be honest about where it comes from.

practice: Hindus keep the story alive by telling it; a telling is called katha. Pick one scene from this week, the deer, the cry, Lakshmana's bow, and tell it in your head in your own words, the way your family would.
If someone's near, tell it to them out loud. Then sit for a few breaths. You're one more teller in a very long line.

wordCard.voice: The line. Lakshman rekha: absent from Valmiki, mentioned by Mandodari in Tulsidas, and now an everyday word for a limit not to be crossed.

orig.note: Hindi lakṣmaṇ rekhā: Lakshmana's line. rekhā means a line or a drawn mark.

carryVoice: Take this with you: many Ramayanas, one Rama. The forest spirits and the line in the dust tell of the same brother's care. See you tomorrow.
